cemc-fryer-2005-02a.prompt:
A game begins with a row of empty boxes. On a turn, a player can put his or her initial in $1$ box or in $2$ adjacent boxes. (Boxes are called *adjacent* if they are next to each other.) Anh and Bharati alternate turns. Whoever initials the last empty box wins the game.

The game begins with a row of $3$ boxes. Anh initials the middle box. Explain why this move guarantees him a win no matter what Bharati does.
cemc-fryer-2005-02a.answer: The two empty boxes are not adjacent, so Bharati can fill only one; Anh fills the last.

cemc-fryer-2005-02b.prompt:
A game begins with a row of empty boxes. On a turn, a player can put his or her initial in $1$ box or in $2$ adjacent boxes. (Boxes are called *adjacent* if they are next to each other.) Anh and Bharati alternate turns. Whoever initials the last empty box wins the game.

Now the game begins with a row of $5$ boxes. Suppose that the following moves have occurred: Anh initialed the middle (3rd) box, then Bharati initialed the 1st (leftmost) box, as shown. Show a move that Anh can make next in order to guarantee that he will win. Explain how this move prevents Bharati from winning.
cemc-fryer-2005-02b.answer: Anh initials the rightmost box (or the 4th box). The two remaining empty boxes are not adjacent, so Bharati takes one and Anh takes the last.

cemc-fryer-2005-02c.prompt:
A game begins with a row of empty boxes. On a turn, a player can put his or her initial in $1$ box or in $2$ adjacent boxes. (Boxes are called *adjacent* if they are next to each other.) Anh and Bharati alternate turns. Whoever initials the last empty box wins the game.

Again the game begins with a row of $5$ boxes. Suppose that Anh has initialed the 2nd box from the left, as shown. Show the two possible moves that Bharati can make next to guarantee she wins. Explain how each of these moves prevents Anh from winning.
cemc-fryer-2005-02c.answer: Bharati initials boxes 4 and 5, or boxes 3 and 4. Either way the two remaining empty boxes are not adjacent, so Anh takes one and Bharati takes the last.

Explain why it is impossible for the line segment $AE$ to have $10$ sub-segments of lengths $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9$, and $10$.
cemc-fryer-2005-04b.answer: The super-sum is $4w + 6x + 6y + 4z$ (always even), but $1 + 2 + \cdots + 10 = 55$ is odd.
